extracted.intended_audience: novice college mathematics instructors; graduate student instructors; pre-service secondary mathematics teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning and running a short faculty meeting on student motivation and for classroom strategies instructors can use to increase students' intrinsic and extrinsic motivation in college mathematics courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit goals the meeting should achieve for participating instructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five listed goals: (1) provide instructors with ideas they can use to motivate students in their teaching situations; (2) provide opportunity to think about what they would like to motivate students to do and how; (3) provide a general description of several motivational strategies, emphasizing instructor as participant in the process; (4) provide opportunity to hear examples from other instructors and ask questions about results observed; (5) provide opportunity to think about ways to increase student confidence and decrease math anxiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation for the meeting (facilitator checklist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical preparatory actions the meeting leader should take to make the session useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items include: check with experienced instructors about what motivating students means and actions they took and results; invite two or three experienced instructors to give three-minute talks addressing specified prompts (what does it mean to motivate students, actions taken, results, future changes); optionally ask participants beforehand about their views and concerns; optionally share participant needs with experienced speakers and tailor handouts; circulate the agenda in advance; make copies of materials and questionnaires and confirm attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agenda for the meeting (topics to cover)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested topical sequence to distribute to participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Five agenda items: outline of general ideas of motivation and implementation; description of departmental strategies and results; opportunity for participants to examine personal meaning of motivation and generate actions; review and discussion of motivational ideas and implementation; discussion of math anxiety and ideas for addressing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for running the meeting (timing & facilitation roles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A detailed minute-by-minute plan for a fifty-minute meeting, including facilitator roles and time allocations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested timeline: :01–:05 introduce meeting and agenda; :05–:20 experienced instructors give talks (facilitator keeps things moving and ensures positive/critical consideration); :20–:30 distribute handout on motivating strategies and provide overview, contrasting short-term/low-commitment strategies with longer-term/higher-commitment ones; :30–:40 lead discussion on math anxiety (identify causes and remedies); :40–:45 participant reflection guided by three questions (outward behavior of motivated student; most/least motivating lessons and why; motivational goals); :45–:50 wrap up, Q&A, summary, further readings, questionnaire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic motivation — definition, statements, advantages, challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: What it means for students to be intrinsically motivated and the pros/cons of relying on intrinsic motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: Students engage because the activity itself is perceived as valuable. Example statements: 'Mathematics interests me.' 'Learning mathematics enables me to think clearly.' Advantages: long-lasting, satisfying to instructors, efforts to motivate are educational, focus on mathematics. Challenges: slow to change behavior, requires preparation, requires multiple approaches for diverse students, can create dependence on instructor, hard to transfer across courses, instructor may need to overcome negative dispositions, instructor must know student interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrinsic motivation — definition, statements, advantages, challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: What it means for students to be extrinsically motivated and the pros/cons of extrinsic strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition: Students act to obtain rewards or avoid penalties associated with engagement rather than valuing the activity itself. Example statements: 'I need a B- to get into Business School.' Advantages: more readily changes behavior, portable across courses, little instructor effort/preparation, does not require extensive knowledge of students. Challenges: can distract from mathematics, hard to devise appropriate rewards/punishments, may require escalation, does not produce long-term motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of intrinsic and extrinsic motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: How intrinsic and extrinsic motivations co-exist and guidance on balancing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: both will always be present — the issue is relative strength; extrinsic rewards can negatively impact intrinsic satisfaction; accept extrinsic motivation as inherent but de-emphasize it and encourage intrinsic motivation; avoid conditions where extrinsic rewards are most damaging: (a) when students would otherwise willingly engage, and (b) when students view rewards as means to manipulate behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grades as an extrinsic strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Considerations for deliberately using course grades to harness student motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations: view tests/assignments as feedback rather than teacher control; grade higher-order learning outcomes (synthesis/evaluation) rather than rote tasks; consider shorter, untimed, or take-home exams to reduce anxiety; use the weakest extrinsic motivators possible (e.g., attendance or late-paper penalties sparingly); use vocabulary framing grades as feedback ('See how well the students are doing').

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter appeals (intrinsic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques to reveal the inherent appeal of mathematics to students to foster intrinsic interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations: teach as if math is interesting and model enthusiasm; expect students to be interested; use cue words/phrases to direct attention to novelty, utility, applicability, anticipation, surprise, challenge, feedback, closure (table of example cue phrases provided); deliberately plan lessons to reveal intrinsic appeal; vary teaching/learning styles; tap students' curiosity using unexpectedness and discovery; emphasize usefulness/applicability of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence (intrinsic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the pursuit of excellence to motivate students and suggested practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: students derive pleasure from doing something well; can pass responsibility for learning to students. Ideas: show enthusiasm for excellent work; create a classroom climate that resists mediocre norms; protect students striving for excellence from criticism; encourage feelings of control over outcomes; for students who fail, emphasize instability of grades and growth potential; maintain standards to give students something to strive for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success-based motivation (intrinsic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Designing opportunities where students can achieve meaningful but attainable success to increase motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations: monitor difficulty of assessments to provide moderate risk of failure for students making progress; develop and communicate positive expectations; give differentiated feedback highlighting strengths and areas to improve and encouraging future outcomes; attribute success to student-controlled causes; use positive vocabulary emphasizing capability rather than blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal setting (intrinsic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using specific, challenging, student-involved goals to motivate productive study behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations: emphasize reaching positive goals rather than avoiding negatives; allow students to develop their own goals; make goals behaviorally specific ('study three hours every evening'); ensure goals are challenging but achievable with effort; help students develop strategies for achieving goals (study skills); encourage periodic review of goals and assessment of current behaviors relative to goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing math anxiety — causes and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of common causes of math anxiety in students and concrete classroom remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems and proposed solutions listed: timed evaluations → allow more time, untimed or take-home exams; fear of forgetting → allow calculators, cheat sheets, or 'purchase' hints for point deduction; competitive classrooms → grade on fixed criterion rather than curve, allow think-time before calling on students, actively involve all students, use cooperative learning; fear of word problems → require many word problems, use familiar contexts, teach problem-solving strategies; unwillingness to flounder → create safe climate for mistakes, convey that struggle is normal, encourage perseverance; weed-out course perception → convey belief that all students can succeed, grade on fixed criterion. Summary guidance: be available and approachable, encourage students, avoid harmful classroom mythology, never belittle students, respect students' struggles and efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novice instructor lesson-planning pitfalls
rubrics_metrics.description: Common limiting tendencies observed in novice college mathematics instructors' lesson planning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported tendencies from research: novice instructors' experiences as learners heavily influence planning; little to no awareness of students' cognitive activity; belief that primary role is to organize content and transmit knowledge → lecture predominates and student activities are sparse; primary objective is to cover material; considerations of assessment are often left out of planning and implementation; belief that most effective student learning occurs outside of class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors relevant to difficult instructor–student situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Points to consider when discussing idiosyncratic or difficult interactions between instructors and particular students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes categories of difficulties: (1) implicit mismatched course expectations; (2) difficulties from nature of interactive classroom; (3) difficulties between individual students and administrative course structure; (4) highly interpersonal situations between instructor and individual students. Facilitator guidance: use scenarios and materials on clear communication. Five relevant contextual points: perception of elementary math as 'weed-out' courses can heighten competition; students hold beliefs about math (memorization, five-minute solutions, etc.) that differ from instructors' beliefs; individuals communicate in varied ways beyond literal verbal content; demographic and attitude changes (older students, part-time jobs, parents) alter student situations; much difficult interaction centers on evaluation and grading — novices may be surprised that some students reject course rules or attempt to work around them.
